newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Taiwan sees no talks with China before July 1997.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan sees no talks with China before July 1997.

text.p: A senior Taiwan official urged China on Monday to restart long-suspended talks with the island, but acknowledged a dialogue was unlikely before Hong Kong returns to Chinese rule in July 1997.

Chiang Pin-kung, chairman of the cabinet's Council for Economic Planning and Development, told Reuters Financial Television that Beijing had no political interest to heed Taipei's call and return to the semi-official bargaining table.
"We are currently waiting for the answer," Chiang said in an interview. "Since they (Beijing) closed the door...they should open it. We never closed the door."

Taiwan and China, rivals since a Chinese civil war separated them in 1949, began a series of semi-official talks in 1993 but Beijing angrily suspended contacts after Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui's high-profile U.S. visit in mid-1995.
Beijing insists that Lee's visit was a move towards Taiwan's independence from China and away from reunification. Both sides say they want to reunify, but under very different terms.

As Taiwan still bans direct contact with China, the island's huge trade and investment in China must be routed through a third region, mostly Hong Kong. That relationship will face its most serious test with the British colony's July return to China.
"We will continue existing relations (with Hong Kong) even after 1997," Chiang said without elaborating how Taiwan's links with Hong Kong could continue once it became part of China.

Chiang also urged the World Trade Organisation not to be swayed by China's political agenda when considering Taiwan's bid to enter. Washington has blocked entry by both China and Taiwan on trade grounds, but China insists on entering before Taiwan.
"The PRC's (China's) situation and our situation should be based on commercial negotiations," Chiang said.
Taiwan has made major concessions in recent years in a bid to join the world body, liberalising trade and privatising many government-controlled industries.

Taiwan has completed obligatory bilateral WTO entry talks with South Africa, Turkey, Malaysia, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary, the Philippines, El Salvador, Colombia, Uruguay and Australia. Those with the United States and Japan would continue, Chiang said.
Taiwan applied in 1990 to join WTO's predecessor, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, under the name Chinese Taipei. WTO replaced GATT in January 1995.
"We hope we can achieve (the goal of entry) some time next year," Chiang said.
